extracted.intended_audience: student journalists / journalism students (high school and college)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing speech reports, reporting letters/reprinted material, and conducting and writing informative interviews for newspapers (especially school and local papers). Covers preparation, structure, quotation usage, sourcing, and ethical cautions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements to note in a speech-report lead
rubrics_metrics.description: From the lead in the first speech report, note the following: (a) speaker, (b) nature of speech, (c) occasion of speech, (d) highlight of the speech, (e) identification of speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lead should identify who spoke, what kind of speech it was, the occasion, the principal point or 'highlight', and provide sufficient identification of the speaker so readers accept their authority. Use this checklist when analyzing or composing a speech report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring speaker back into the report
rubrics_metrics.description: Note the ways that the speaker is brought back into the speech; how often and by what verbal devices the writer recalls the speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain the speaker in the reader's mind throughout the report by periodically referring to them (name, titles, pronouns, descriptive nouns). Vary verbs used instead of 'said' to avoid repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct vs. indirect discourse in speech reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of direct and indirect discourse (quotations and paraphrase) when reporting a speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose direct quotations for striking or characteristic language; use indirect discourse to save words and summarize. Be aware of economy and clarity when mixing both forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy / economical devices in speech reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should use economic devices to save words, e.g., indirect discourse, compressed summaries, and judicious selection of quotes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect and apply economical devices (ellipsis, paraphrase, summary leads) so the report remains concise while retaining key highlights and representative phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formula for reporting a letter
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple formula for reporting the letter follows: 1. Summary lead identifying the writer as a person to be listened to; occasion of the letter. 2. Brief statement to introduce the letter or parts of the letter. 3. The letter, or parts of it, quoted exactly as written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reprinting letters, lead with the writer's authority and occasion, introduce context, then quote verbatim the portions being published. Use this order for clarity and news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not publish personal letters without consent
rubrics_metrics.description: No personal letter, of course, should ever be made public without the consent of the writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ethical requirement: obtain permission before making private correspondence public. Verify consent before reprinting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give credit to the source for reprinted material
rubrics_metrics.description: Similar use is often made of material that has already been printed, but full credit must be given to the publication from which it has been taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always identify the original publication and explicitly state whether material is quoted in whole or in part. Proper attribution preserves credibility and avoids plagiarism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of indirect discourse for rehashed printed sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect discourse may be used if the matter is presented unmistakably as from another source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When 'rehashing' circulars, reports, journals, or other printed sources, paraphrase economically but make clear the source; use indirect quotation to condense while indicating attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of written sources suitable for reworking
rubrics_metrics.description: Circulars, statistical reports, technical journals, current magazines, bulletins, and newspapers often furnish material for 'rehashing' into popular articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should identify relevant printed sources and adapt material with clear attribution and appropriate selection for their audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of the informative interview
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of the informative interview is to get before the reader information or opinion or advice from a recognized authority on the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on extracting and presenting facts, opinions, or advice from an accepted authority rather than on descriptive color, setting, or the interviewee's appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of persons to interview for information
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons to interview for information: persons of unquestioned importance; persons of influence; accepted authorities; the expert; one who has achieved distinction in any field; any reliable person who can talk on the new, the strange, the picturesque, the unexpected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select interviewees whose position, expertise, or experience gives news value and authority to the material. Justify selection to readers (identify why they are an authority).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation before the interview
rubrics_metrics.description: BEFORE THE INTERVIEW: 1. Inform yourself of at least the high points of the subject. 2. Get the correct full name of the person to be interviewed. 3. Inform yourself as to why he is an accepted authority on the subject. 4. Prepare questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research the topic and the person so questions are informed and focused. Know the interviewee's credentials and prepare a prioritized question list to guide the conversation.

rubrics_metrics.name: During-the-interview technique
rubrics_metrics.description: DURING THE INTERVIEW: 1. Note the significant remarks. 2. Try to catch exact phrases or sentences. 3. Get all the information needed in your article. 4. If the person interviewed rambles, bring him back tactfully. 5. Be insistent but courteous. 6. Don't miss chance remarks that have news value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listen actively, record or take careful notes of key quotes and facts, steer the interview back to relevant topics when needed, and politely probe for specifics. Be alert for unexpected newsworthy comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: After-the-interview steps
rubrics_metrics.description: AFTER THE INTERVIEW: Review the speaker's remarks and put them into your notebook at once. Stand off from the interview and pick out the most significant or striking remark, or decide what facts best summarize the interview. Put this representative statement first when you begin to write.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transcribe or organize notes immediately to avoid loss. Identify the 'representative statement' or highlight to use as lead; prioritize elements for the story's structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple plan for organizing the interview story
rubrics_metrics.description: SIMPLE PLAN FOR ORGANIZING THE INTERVIEW STORY: 1. Summary lead (opinion/statement by person interviewed, identify him as an accepted authority, include occasion). 2. Direct quotation. 3. Indirect quotation. 4. Brief direct quotation to conclude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this structural order to combine authoritative lead, illustrative direct quotes for life, indirect paraphrase for economy, and a closing quote to end emphatically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautions on mixing quotation forms and voice
rubrics_metrics.description: CAUTIONS: Don't mix direct and indirect quotations in the same paragraph. Keep the person interviewed in the mind of your readers by referring to him throughout the report. Get a list of nouns to use instead of his name. Don’t use said too often. Never use the first person even to suggest your questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain clarity by separating direct quotes from paraphrase; vary noun references and attribution verbs; avoid the reporter's first-person presence in the text; preserve narrative flow and objectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put the highlight into the lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Put the High Light Into the Lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the opening sentence emphasize the most newsworthy or striking element of the speech or interview to engage readers immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: If interviewing outside the school, justify inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Note.—If you interview some one outside your school for your paper, you must make a point of contact between that person or his subject and your school life, to justify the appearance of the interview in a school paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When publishing interviews of outsiders in a school/local paper, explicitly link the subject to the audience's interests to establish relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic forms: dateline usage (example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain journalistic forms are constantly used. Example dateline: 'Doorn, Holland, Jan. 25 (AP).—' followed by a concise opening paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use standard dateline format to indicate location and wire service when appropriate; follow with a concise lead that adheres to news style and economy.
